judge_assessment.explanation: The judge's arithmetic is exact. worksheet.tex defines \tenframe{top}{bottom} and the ten problems instantiate it as {5}{1}, {5}{4}, {4}{4}, {5}{2}, {5}{5}, {5}{2} vs {5}{4}, {2}{2}, {3}{2}, {4}{4} vs {5}{3}, {5}{1} vs {5}{4} — giving 6, 9, 8, 3 empty, 10, 7<9, 6 needed, 5, 8=8, and empty counts 4 > 1. That is the judge's list item for item, and each matches verify.json (ids 4, 7 and 10 correctly compute against empties: '10 - a - b' and values ['10-6','10-9']). The dots are drawn by a parameterised tikz macro rather than typed, so the figures cannot disagree with the declared counts, which supports the judge's legibility finding as well. I part company only on answer_key_quality 4/4: the delivered Quick Answers bank prints '6. —', '9. —' and '10. —', the three verified compare relations ('<', '=', '>'), even though this key has no manual items — the judge did not open the bank.

strengths_to_preserve: Problems 1, 2 and 5 build the habit 'the top row is full, so start at five', and problem 8 then breaks it deliberately: \tenframe{3}{2} with the stem 'Careful — the top row is not full', and a declared trap for the child who assumed five and added three (value 7, machine-proved distinguishable from 5). Teaching a shortcut and then testing whether the child checks its precondition is exactly what a fluency ramp should do.

The set pivots three times on what is being counted — filled cells (1, 2, 3, 5, 8), empty cells (4, 7), and then a comparison of EMPTY cells in problem 10 ('10-6' against '10-9') — so ten items share one representation without repeating a problem skeleton, which is what the prompt asked for.

Every frame is emitted by the single \tenframe{#1}{#2} macro defined at the top of worksheet.tex, so the picture is generated from the same two numbers the verify entry uses. There is no hand-placed dot anywhere on the sheet that could drift from the answer key.

root_causes.description: The three comparison problems are verified relations, but render_quick_answers._fmt formats a string expected through bare sympy.sympify, which raises on '<', '=' and '>', so all three bank rows fall through to the '---' that render_entry also uses for manual-only problems. On this sheet nothing is manual, so all three dashes are false blanks — including problem 10, whose answer is the subtlest on the page (comparing empty cells rather than dots) and therefore the one a grader is most likely to look up.

improvements.title: Quick Answers must typeset a verified relation instead of the manual-only em dash
improvements.proposed_change: In scripts/render_quick_answers.py, handle relation expecteds before the sympify fallback in _fmt: when a problem entry is type 'compare' with order 'relation', map the expected string '<', '>', '=', '<=', '>=', '!=' onto its LaTeX glyph ($<$, $>$, $=$, $\le$, $\ge$, $\ne$) and, where the compare 'values' are literals, print the resolved comparison (e.g. '$12 < 15$') so the bank row carries the same information as the worked solution. Reserve '---' exclusively for problems whose only entries are type 'manual', and add a build warning when _fmt would emit '---' for a non-manual entry, so a future silent drop is loud. Keep this fix separate from the sympify-sandbox fix (quick-answers-must-not-typeset-python-builtins) — that one must REJECT a non-mathematical object, this one must RENDER a relation.
improvements.regression_test: Add to tests/test_render_quick_answers.py a fixture verify JSON holding one {'id':1,'type':'compare','order':'relation','expected':'<'} entry and one {'id':2,'type':'manual','desc':...} entry, then assert the generated bank contains a typeset '<' on row 1 and '---' on row 2, and that row 1 is not '---'. Today row 1 renders '---' (sympify('<') raises SympifyError and _fmt falls through), so the assertion fails before the fix and passes after. Cases in this run that the test reproduces: curr-007 problems 6, 9 and 10.
improvements.expected_impact: Every verified inequality/equality answer becomes visible in the answer key's fast-checking bank, and the em dash regains its single meaning ('nobody machine-checked this'), so a grader can tell a verified relation from a genuine manual item at a glance.
improvements.risk: Low. The change is confined to formatting one expected value; existing numeric, list and dict rows are untouched. The only visible difference is that rows previously blank now print a glyph, which can widen a bank column and re-flow column_count — worth asserting the column arithmetic in the same test.

case_summary: A clean, fully correct ten-frame fluency packet. I re-derived all ten answers from the \tenframe arguments in worksheet.tex and every one matches verify.json and the key: 6, 9, 8, 3 empty, 10, 7<9, 6 needed, 5, 8=8, 4>1. The ramp is real — filled cells, then empty cells, then comparisons, then a comparison of empties — and problem 8 deliberately breaks the 'top row is full' shortcut the earlier items install, with the corresponding misconception declared and machine-checked. Because every frame is drawn by one parameterised macro from the same numbers the verifier uses, there is no way for a picture to disagree with an answer. The single defect is in the answer key's Quick Answers bank, which prints an em dash for the three verified relation answers — the glyph that elsewhere means 'no machine checked this'. The worked solutions carry the relations correctly, so this is a delivery defect in the fast-checking bank rather than a mathematical one.
